reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A congenital, non-neoplastic malformation of disorganised but mature neurons and glia arising in the region of the tuber cinereum and mammillary bodies
The classic presentation combines gelastic (laughing) seizures with central precocious puberty
Gelastic seizures often begin in infancy and can be subtle, sometimes dismissed as normal laughter
Sessile lesions with a broad intrahypothalamic attachment are more strongly associated with intractable epilepsy, while pedunculated lesions more often present with precocious puberty
Over time an epileptic encephalopathy can develop, with additional seizure types, cognitive decline and behavioural disturbance including aggression
MRI shows a non-enhancing mass isointense to grey matter that does not change over time, helping distinguish it from a tumour
Precocious puberty is treatable hormonally, and drug-resistant seizures may respond to surgical, laser or radiosurgical approaches targeting the lesion
reference.pathophysiology: Hypothalamic hamartoma is a congenital heterotopic mass of intrinsically epileptogenic neuronal and glial tissue located at the tuber cinereum. Intralesional small GABAergic-type neurons can fire autonomously, generating seizures within the lesion itself, which then propagate through hypothalamic and limbic networks to produce gelastic and other seizures. The lesion's disruption of hypothalamic regulation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis drives central precocious puberty, and some cases are associated with somatic GLI3 pathway variants or with syndromic disorders such as Pallister-Hall syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Temporal or frontal lobe epilepsy from other causes
Tuberous sclerosis or other structural epileptogenic lesions
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with dedicated hypothalamic views to characterise a non-enhancing grey-matter-isointense mass
Endocrine evaluation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis for precocious puberty
Electroencephalography and video-EEG to characterise gelastic and other seizures
Neuropsychological assessment for cognitive and behavioural comorbidity
Genetic evaluation where a syndromic association such as Pallister-Hall is suspected
Serial imaging to confirm lesion stability and exclude neoplasm
redFlags: Progressive epileptic encephalopathy with cognitive regression and behavioural deterioration
Drug-resistant seizures affecting development and quality of life
Signs of a growing or enhancing mass suggesting an alternative neoplastic diagnosis
Endocrine disturbance beyond precocious puberty indicating wider hypothalamic dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Precocious puberty is generally well controlled with hormonal therapy. The epilepsy outlook depends on lesion type and size: some remain mild, but sessile intrahypothalamic lesions can produce a progressive epileptic encephalopathy, and in these cases targeted surgical, laser ablation or radiosurgical treatment offers the best chance of seizure control and cognitive stabilisation.
pitfalls: Mistaking early gelastic seizures for normal or emotional laughter and delaying diagnosis
Misinterpreting the lesion as a neoplasm and pursuing unnecessary oncological management
Attempting to control intractable seizures with medication alone when disconnection or ablation is more effective
Overlooking central precocious puberty as a clue when seizures dominate the presentation
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
